disclaimer: Decision support only. These notes were written for a student prototype and reviewed against publicly documented guidance on Ugandan banana production. Only a qualified officer or laboratory test can confirm a diagnosis.

conditions.name: Banana Xanthomonas Wilt (BXW)
conditions.summary: A bacterial disease that can destroy a whole matooke stand within a season. It blocks the water-conducting vessels, so the plant wilts and the fruit ripens prematurely and dries out.
spread: Contaminated pruning knives, pangas and hoes moved from an infected plant
Banana hopper insects visiting male buds
Run-off water and soil moved on boots or animals
Suckers taken from an infected garden
favouring_conditions: Working in the garden while plants and soil are wet
Sharing tools between gardens without disinfecting
immediate_actions: Mark the affected plant and stop touching neighbouring plants with the same tool
Cut the pseudostem about 30 cm above ground in a dry period, leave it standing and do not move infected material
Cut out and bag the male bud and any infected fruit, then dispose of the bag safely
Disinfect the knife between every plant (household bleach 1 part to 4 parts water, or 90 % alcohol; soak/wipe and let it dry)
Cover the cut pseudostem with a small bag of bleach-soaked cloth or plastic so insects cannot carry bacteria onward
prevention: Remove and destroy the male bud (bud deactivation) on all plants in the mat - this removes the insect route
Prune and de-leaf regularly so the mat is dry and easy to inspect
Use clean planting material: tissue-culture plantlets or treated sword suckers only
Do not enter a neighbour's garden with tools used in an infected garden
Control weeds and avoid water flowing into a healthy mat
Isolate the infected mat and keep a sanitation record so you can show officials what you did
explain_what_may_be_wrong: Male buds were left on the plants, so insects could move bacteria between bunches
Tools were used across plants or gardens without disinfecting
Infected leaves, buds or stems were carried across the garden
Suckers were taken from a garden that already had the disease
conditions.seek_help: Report it to your parish/district agricultural officer promptly. BXW is a notified problem and control is a community action - your neighbours' gardens matter as much as yours.

references.title: Banana Xanthomonas Wilt management guidance (National Banana Research Institute, Nzerekore)
references.source: NVRI / NARO - verify current version with your district

references.title: Integrated BXW management: male bud removal, tool disinfection, sanitation

conditions.name: Black Sigatoka (leaf spot)
conditions.summary: A leaf fungus that kills the leaf area the plant needs to fill the bunch. It usually starts as small streaks or spots on the underside of the youngest fully open leaf and matures into dark lesions with pale centres.
spread: Spores carried by wind and rain splash from infected leaves
Old infected leaves and leaf debris left in the garden
favouring_conditions: Frequent rain and long leaf-wetness, warm temperatures
Infected leaves left hanging on the plant
immediate_actions: Remove the most badly spotted leaves and pull them out of the garden - do not drop them between plants
Improve air flow: thin the mat so one or two healthy stems remain per hole
Open drains where water stands; prune leaves touching the ground

Where the garden is large and loss is real, a protectant fungicide (for example copper-based, or a systemic product from an agro-dealer) can help - rotate active ingredients, follow the label, and spray in the evening. Do not spray near water sources or without protective clothing.
Do not harvest or eat fruit from leaves sprayed within the product's waiting period
prevention: Regular de-leafing and de-suckering (sanitation) is the cheapest control
Plant at recommended spacing (roughly 3 x 3 m for matooke on good land) rather than tighter
Keep drainage channels open before the long rains
Maintain soil fertility, especially potassium through ash or compost where a soil test supports it
Scout the youngest fully opened leaf every week and act on the first streaks
explain_what_may_be_wrong: Old infected leaves were left on the plant, so spores kept reinfecting new leaves
Plants are too crowded and the garden stays wet
No regular de-leafing or de-suckering was done
Fertility has fallen, making leaves soft and more easily infected
conditions.seek_help: An extension worker can estimate disease severity on the standard 1-6 lesion scale and advise whether spraying is economic for your plot.

references.title: Sigatoka management in banana: sanitation, spacing, nutrition, fungicide resistance management

conditions.name: Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV)
conditions.causal_agent: Banana bunchy top virus, spread by the banana aphid Pentalonia nigronervosa
conditions.summary: A virus with no cure. The plant is stunted, leaves become narrow, cup upward at the edges and cluster at the top like a rosette; dark green streaks run along the veins of the midrib and leaf stalk.
spread: Banana aphids moving from infected to healthy plants
Infected suckers used as planting material
Volunteer plants and ratoons left from an infected mat
favouring_conditions: Ants tending aphids on the pseudostem
Old, neglected mats with ratoons and volunteers
Planting material from a garden with the disease
immediate_actions: Do not spray hoping to cure the plant - infected plants stay infected
Inject or spot-treat the plant with an insecticide so aphids leave before you cut it, then cut and kill the plant and all its suckers (this is the standard 'destroy then disinfect' approach)
Cover the cut stump and remove the corm so new ratoons do not carry the virus
Disinfect tools and boots afterwards
Control ants and aphids on the remaining healthy mats
prevention: Plant only clean tissue-culture material or suckers from a disease-free, inspected source
Rogue out infected plants as soon as symptoms appear - early removal protects the whole garden
Keep the garden free of volunteers and ratoons
Avoid ant nests climbing the pseudostem (they protect aphids)
explain_what_may_be_wrong: Suckers were taken from an infected garden
Symptomatic plants were left standing 'to finish the bunch'
Weeding and mat cleaning were skipped, so aphids and ants built up
conditions.seek_help: BBTV needs a verified response because removal of whole mats is involved. Contact the district agricultural officer; samples can be tested by immunostaining/PCR at a national laboratory.

references.title: BBTV management: insecticide treatment before removal, clean planting material, rogueing

conditions.name: Moko / blood disease (bacterial wilt complex)
conditions.causal_agent: Ralstonia solanacearum race 2 (blood disease in Asia)
conditions.summary: Looks very close to BXW: sudden wilting, blackened vascular tissue inside the stem and petioles, and shrivelled immature fruit. In Uganda BXW is far more likely, but the field response is similar and the distinction matters for reporting.
spread: Tools, water, and infected planting material
Contact with tomato, potato or pepper land carrying the bacterium
immediate_actions: Treat it like BXW until a laboratory says otherwise: isolate, disinfect, remove plant material
Do not plant matooke where tomato or potato was recently grown without soil inspection
prevention: Clean planting material, drainage, crop separation from solanaceous crops, tool hygiene
explain_what_may_be_wrong: Planting material came from an unknown source
Land previously under tomato/potato was used without checking
conditions.seek_help: Laboratory differentiation from BXW is required. Involve the district agricultural officer.

conditions.name: Burrowing / root-knot nematodes
conditions.causal_agent: Radopholus similis, Pratylenchus spp., Meloidogyne spp.
conditions.summary: Microscopic worms attack the roots and corm. The plant cannot take up water and nutrients, so bunches are small, plants yellow slowly, and in wind the whole plant topples because roots are weakened.
spread: Infested soil moved on tools, water or planting material
Continuous banana cropping with no rotation
favouring_conditions: Land previously cropped with grasses or solanaceous hosts
immediate_actions: Improve organic matter: well-rotted manure or compost applied around the mat
Mulch heavily to protect soil life and moisture
Improve drainage where water stands
Hot-water treatment (about 50 C for 15-20 minutes) of planting material is the standard low-cost disinfestation - get the timing right or you cook the sucker
prevention: Use clean, inspected planting material
Rotate neglected land with maize, beans or marigold before replanting
Keep soil fertility and organic matter high
Avoid moving soil between gardens on tools or boots
explain_what_may_be_wrong: Suckers came from an infested garden
Land was replanted to banana continuously without rotation or organic inputs
Soil fertility and organic matter have collapsed
conditions.seek_help: A soil sample tested at a laboratory tells you whether nematodes are the real limit, before you spend on any chemical nematicide.

references.title: Nematode management in banana: hot-water treatment, sanitation, rotation

conditions.name: Banana weevil / corm weevil
conditions.summary: The adult beetle bores into the base of the plant and the larvae tunnel inside the corm. You see notched leaf edges, holes at the pseudostem base, and weak plants that fall over.
spread: Infected planting material with corm attached
Old stumps and debris left in the garden
favouring_conditions: Mulch of fresh, infested pseudostem left on the ground
immediate_actions: Split infested pseudostems into pieces and place them as pitfall traps at ground level; collect trapped weevils every 2-3 days and destroy them
Remove and burn or deeply bury old stumps and corm debris
Trim and inspect suckers before planting, removing any with tunnels
Practise 'cut and spread': cut the infested stem, spread the pieces to dry so larvae die
prevention: Clean planting material and careful sucker inspection
Sanitation of stumps after harvesting
Trapping kept up year-round, not once
Mulch with dry, weevil-free material
explain_what_may_be_wrong: Stumps were left in the field after the previous harvest, giving weevils a breeding site
Planting material was not trimmed or inspected
Fresh green mulch was used
conditions.seek_help: An extension worker can show you trap density and, for heavy infestation, whether a labelled biological or chemical drench is economic for your plot.

references.title: Integrated weevil management: traps, sanitation, clean planting material

conditions.name: Potassium (and general fertility) deficiency
conditions.causal_agent: Low available soil potassium / depleted soil
conditions.summary: Not a disease, but it looks like one. Older leaf edges yellow then scorch and dry, bunches fill poorly, fingers stay thin, and the plant is weaker against Sigatoka and wind.
favouring_conditions: Old, continuously cropped gardens with no manure or fertiliser
Sandy soils, or very acidic soils
Removing residues and each harvest taking nutrients away
immediate_actions: Apply well-rotted manure or compost around the mat (not against the stem)
Add wood ash where available and soil is not already alkaline - it supplies potassium but test first
Mulch to hold moisture and feed soil life
Do not broadcast fertiliser on a waterlogged or bone-dry soil; work it into the wetted zone
prevention: Return residues (outer sheaths, dead leaves) to the mat
Annual organic inputs, plus a soil test every few years
Liming only where a test shows acidity
explain_what_may_be_wrong: Nothing has been returned to the soil for several seasons
Fertiliser applied at the wrong time or in the wrong place
Soil pH is locking up nutrients
conditions.seek_help: A soil test is cheap relative to fertiliser you may waste. District laboratories and NARO can advise rates.

conditions.name: Waterlogging / root asphyxia
conditions.summary: Standing water or compacted soil suffocates roots. Leaves yellow from the oldest upward, growth stalls, plants look generally soft, and root rot organisms follow.
favouring_conditions: land at the bottom of a slope
immediate_actions: Open drainage channels around and through the garden before the next rain
Avoid walking on wet plots (compaction)
Do not apply nitrogen while roots are damaged - it adds stress
prevention: Plant on mounds or in raised beds on heavy soils
Keep drains cleared each season
Add organic matter to improve structure
explain_what_may_be_wrong: The plot has no outlets and drains were never cut
Soil structure collapsed from continuous cropping and trampling
conditions.seek_help: Water management is a landscape problem - discuss it with the parish agricultural development officer, ideally with neighbouring gardens.

references.title: Drainage and land preparation for banana in humid highland zones

conditions.name: Sunscald / heat and wind damage
conditions.causal_agent: Excessive radiation, dry wind, leaf loss
conditions.summary: When too few leaves shade the bunch, the peel bleaches, blushes or splits and the fingers stop filling. Often follows aggressive de-leafing, a dry windy season, or leaf loss from Sigatoka.
immediate_actions: Leave enough functional leaves - roughly 8-12 healthy leaves per stem supports bunch filling and shade
Prop or tie bunches in windy spots, keep a leaf sheath around the bunch where practical
Plant windbreaks (Grevillea, Calliandra) on exposed edges
prevention: Prune for balance, not appearance
Maintain windbreaks and intercrop canopy
Irrigate or mulch in dry spells where feasible
explain_what_may_be_wrong: Too many leaves were removed during 'cleaning'
The plot is exposed on a ridge or open lake shore
conditions.seek_help: None needed unless the damage is severe; adjust pruning practice.

references.title: Banana bunch protection and leaf retention

questions.text: How fast did the problem appear?

options.label: Very fast - within a week or two
Gradually, over several weeks or months

questions.text: Which plants in the garden are affected?

options.label: One plant, or a few next to each other
Many plants across the garden, looking similar

questions.text: What is happening to the fruit/bunch?

options.label: It ripens early, shrivels and dries before maturity
It is small, thin and fills poorly
No bunch yet / fruit looks normal

questions.text: Look at the male bud (the 'heart') - what do you see?

options.label: It is turning black, drying or oozing
It looks normal, or I removed it

questions.text: If you cut the stem (or a leaf stalk) lengthwise, what does the inside look like?
What is the main problem on the leaves?

options.label: Spots, streaks or lesions (often with a pale centre or yellow edge)
Yellowing and drying, starting at the edges
Small, narrow, cupped leaves crowded at the top

questions.text: Are plants falling over, especially after wind?

options.label: Yes, they topple or lean badly

questions.text: Have you seen insects or damage at the base of the plant?

options.label: Notches on leaves, holes or tunnels at the base / beetles under the cut stem
Small dark insects clustered near the top / on young leaves, often with ants

questions.text: What is the garden and weather like?

options.label: Very wet, water stands, or lots of rain recently
Old garden, no manure or fertiliser for years

questions.text: If you can see roots or the corm, do they look damaged?
